div.p: Hymn in Honour of the Holy Martyrs Emeterius and Chelidonius of Calahorra.
The names of two martyrs are written in heaven,
which Christ has inscribed there in letters of gold,
and the same he has given to earth, written in marks of blood.
By this lineage the blessed Spanish land flourishes the world over,
this place God saw as worthy to hold their bones,
a chaste host fit to keep their blessed bodies.
Here, stained by a twofold slaughter, the ground drank the warm streams,
and now the dwellers throng the sands steeped in holy gore,
imploring with voice, with vows, with offerings.
From abroad too the settler of the world comes hither,
for rumour, the betrayer, has run through every land
that here are patrons of mankind whom suppliants may surround.
No one here, in his asking, has ever heaped up pure prayers in vain;
glad the suppliant returns from here, his weeping wiped away,
feeling that all he justly asked for has been granted.
So great is the care of these advocates for our perils,
they let no one pour out a single murmur of the voice in vain,
but hear it, and at once bear it to the ear of the eternal King.
Thence from the very fountainhead gifts flow in abundance to the earth,
which water the suppliants’ causes with the remedies they sought.
Never has good Christ denied anything to his own witnesses,
witnesses whom neither chains nor cruel death could frighten
from confessing the one God at the cost of their blood—
blood, yet a longer light repays so great a loss.
This kind of death is glorious, this worthy of upright men:
to give to the enemy’s sword the limbs that disease would have devoured,
woven of failing veins, and by death to conquer the foe.
A beautiful thing it is to suffer the stroke beneath the persecutor’s blade.
Through the wide wound a noble gate is opened to the just:
the soul, washed in the red fount, leaps out from its seat in the heart.
Nor had they led, before, a life untried by hard toil,
these soldiers whom Christ calls to the everlasting belt of service;
their valour, schooled in war and arms, now fights in sacred shrines.
They leave the standards of Caesar, they choose the sign of the cross,
and in place of the windblown banners of the dragons they once bore
they carry the glorious wood before them, the wood that crushed the dragon.
They count it base to bear javelins in their ready right hands,
to batter a wall with engines, to ring a camp with trenches,
to stain impious hands with bloody slaughter.
By chance then a fierce commander of the worldly court
had ordered the second offspring of Israel to go to the altar,
to make sacrifice to the dark idols, to become deserters of Christ.
A plague girt with steel pressed hard upon their free faith;
but that faith, brave, sought out of its own accord the rods,
the axes, the cloven claws, undaunted in the love of Christ.
The prison fetters their necks bound fast with hard rings;
the torturer plies his barbarous hands through all the forum;
truth is reckoned a crime, the faithful voice is punished.
Then valour, cut down by the sword, struck the grim ground,
and, cast upon the mournful pyres, drank in the flames with its mouth.
Then sweet it was to the just to be burned, sweet to endure the steel.
Here the dear hearts of two brothers grow warm together,
whom a faithful comradeship had joined through all their days.
They stand ready to bear whatever the last lot might bring,
whether the neck must be offered to the public axe
after the force of the cracking lash, after the racks of fire,
or the breast must be thrown to the leopards or the lions.
“Shall we, begotten for Christ, be dedicated to Mammon,
and, bearing the image of God, be slaves to the world?
Far be it that the heavenly fire should mingle itself with darkness.
Let it suffice that our life, seized under the first bond,
has paid every debt, having discharged what was Caesar’s;
it is time that what is God’s own be repaid to God.
Go, masters of the standards; and you, tribunes, stand aside.
Take away your golden collars, the rewards of the wounded!
Already from here the bright wages of the angels call us.
There Christ presides over cohorts robed in white,
and, reigning from his high throne, he condemns the infamous gods
and you, who fashion for yourselves laughable monsters as deities.”
As they speak these words the martyrs are crushed with a thousand torments;
a twisting rigour wraps both their hands in bonds,
and steel rings their chafed necks with heavy circles.
O the worn-out oblivion of a silent age!
These deeds are begrudged us, and their very fame is snuffed out.
For a blasphemous henchman once carried off the records,
lest the ages, instructed by enduring books,
should scatter through the ears of those to come
the order, the time, the manner of the passion handed down by sweet tongues.
Yet this alone the old silences withhold from us:
whether they fed their long hair under unbroken chains,
with what pain the torturer, with what parade, arrayed the men.
But this praise is not hidden, nor does it grow old with time:
that gifts, sent upward through the air, flew away,
gifts that, gleaming ahead, would show the way of heaven lying open.
Figuring the faith of one, a ring is borne upon a cloud;
the other gives, they say, a kerchief as pledge of his lips,
and these, snatched up by a breath from on high, enter the inmost light.
Through the axis of the flowing sky the flash of gold is hidden,
and the white of the cloth long flees the eye that follows it;
they are borne up even to the stars and are seen no more.
The crowd standing by saw this; the executioner himself saw it
and held back his hand, faltering, and grew pale with amazement;
yet still he carried through the stroke, lest the glory should be lost.
Do you believe now, you brutish heathenry of the Basques of old,
what sacred blood your cruel error sacrifices?
Do you believe that the souls of victims are carried up to God?
See how openly the fierce demons are tamed here,
who, seizing in wolfish fashion, devour men’s hearts,
strangle minds, and mingle themselves with the very senses.
Then, now full of his foe, the man is set there raving,
breathing out foaming spittle, twisting his savage eyes,
to be cleansed by an examination not of his own crimes.
You may hear—though no torturer stands by—the piteous wailings;
the body is torn under the scourge, yet no scourge is seen,
and the man himself, hung up, swells under hidden bonds.
By such means the martyrs’ power shakes the filthy robber,
this restrains him, racks, burns, this strikes him with chains;
the plunderer, tormented, strips himself from the marrow he had left.
He leaves the prey unharmed, he flees with dry jaws,
from the bottom of the nail to the hair he gives all back whole,
confessing that he himself burns; for he is a dweller in hell.
Why should I tell of bodies cleansed of long diseases and made white,
when a cold shuddering shakes the discoloured limbs,
here a swelling leaves the face, here the true colour returns?
This good the Saviour himself granted us to enjoy,
when he consecrated the limbs of the martyrs to our town,
which now keep safe the dwellers whom the Ebro washes.
Stand now and sing the hymn, you mothers, for your little ones recovered;
let the glad voice of wedded wives ring out for their husbands’ safety:
let this day be a feast for us, let it be a hallowed joy!
Hymn in Honour of the Passion of Lawrence, Most Blessed Martyr.
Ancient mother of pagan shrines,
Rome now given over to Christ,
victorious with Lawrence for your leader,
you triumph over the barbarous rite.
You had conquered proud kings
and curbed whole peoples with the bridle;
now upon the monstrous idols
you lay the yoke of your empire.
This glory alone was lacking
to the honours of the toga-clad city,
that, having captured the savagery of the nations,
it should tame the filthy Jove—
not by the turbulent strength
of Cossus, Camillus, or Caesar,
but by the martyr Lawrence
in a battle not without blood.
Faith fought in arms,
lavish of its own gore;
for by death it destroyed death,
and spent itself upon itself.
The priest had foretold this would be,
Xystus, already nailed to the cross,
seeing Lawrence weeping
at the very foot of the cross:
“Cease at my departure
to pour out tears in grief!
I go before, brother; you too
will follow after three days.”
The bishop’s last word,
herald of his glory,
failed in nothing: for the foretold
day brought the palm.
With what voice, with what praises
shall I celebrate the order of his death?
In what song shall I sing,
worthily retracing his passion?
He, first of the seven men
who stand nearest the altar,
a deacon high in rank
and surpassing the rest,
presided over the sacred enclosures,
governing the secret of the heavenly house
with faithful keys,
and dispensing the wealth vowed to God.
The prefect of the royal city
turns over his hunger for money,
minister of a maddened ruler,
an exactor of gold and of blood,
by what force he may dig out the hidden
coins, supposing that talents
lie covered beneath the sanctuaries
and that heaped-up hoards are concealed.
He orders Lawrence to be brought,
demanding the chest crammed with rich
ingots and the mountains of gleaming
coined money laid up in store.
“You are wont,” he says, “to complain
that we rage more than is just,
when we cut Christian bodies
more cruelly than blood allows.
No fervent severity is found
in these more atrocious commotions;
gently and quietly I demand
what you ought to undergo of your own will.
It has been disclosed that this is the custom
and the practice handed down in your rites,
this the discipline of your covenant,
that the priests make offering of gold.
They say that the sacred blood smokes
in cups of silver,
and that in the nightly rites
fixed candles stand upon gold.
Then it is the brethren’s chief care,
as the talkative report attests,
to offer, when their lands are sold,
thousands of sesterces.
The estates of their grandfathers, made over
under base auctions,
the disinherited heir bewails,
left needy for his holy parents.
These things are hidden in the secret
corners of the churches,
and it is held the highest piety
to strip one’s sweet children bare.
Bring forth the treasures which, by wicked
and deceitful tricks of persuasion,
you hold heaped together,
which you shut up in a blackening cave.
This the public service requires,
this the treasury, this the exchequer,
that money assigned to the soldiers’ pay
may aid the ruler.
So is your doctrine, I hear:
render to each man his own.
Lo, Caesar recognizes his own
stamp set upon the coins.
What you know to be Caesar’s, give
to Caesar—surely I ask what is just;
unless I am mistaken, your God
stamps no money at all,
nor, when he came, did he bring down
golden Philips with him,
but gave his precepts in words,
empty of any purse.
Fulfil the pledge of those sayings
by which you peddle yourselves through the world:
gladly give back the coins,
be rich in words alone.”
Lawrence brings back to these
nothing harsh or troubled,
but, as one ready to comply,
he nods his obedient assent.
“He is rich,” he says, “I do not deny it;
our Church possesses
great store of wealth and gold,
nor is anyone in the world richer.
Augustus himself does not have
so much of those silver tokens,
though he holds the citadel of empire,
and every coin is inscribed to him.
Yet I do not refuse to bring forth
the chest of a wealthy deity;
I will make all things known and bring out
the precious things that Christ holds.
But one thing I ask, in prayer:
a little space of truce,
that I may more effectively discharge
the duty of my promise,
while all the furniture of Christ
is set down for me in order;
for first the small sum must be reckoned,
then noted down.”
The prefect swells with gladness,
glad, and devours his hope,
exulting as if the gold, already
stored at home, were waiting.
They fixed a term of three days;
commended then, Lawrence
is released, surety for himself
and surety of a vast profit.
For three days he runs about the city,
driving the feeble companies
and all who ask for alms
into one place, gathering them together.
There, displaying to both his eyes
hollowed sockets,
one with a guiding staff was steering
his step that wandered in blindness;
another, lame with a broken knee
or half-footed with a maimed leg,
or with one sole shorter than the other,
dragged an uneven gait.
There is one with ulcerous limbs
that drip with corrupting decay,
one whose withered right hand
draws its sinews up to the elbow.
Such men he seeks in every street,
used to be fed
from the store of mother Church,
whom he himself, as steward, had known.
Then he reviews them one by one,
writing each man’s name,
and bids them, set in a long row,
stand before the temple.
And now the appointed day
had passed: the judge raged hot,
with a greedy spirit,
demanding that the promise be paid.
Then the martyr: “I would have you stand by
and marvel at the wealth set out
before you, which our God
most rich possesses in his saints.
You will see a vast hall
gleaming with vessels of gold,
and through the open porticoes
rows built up of talents.”
He goes, and is not ashamed to follow;
they came to the consecrated door,
where stood the throngs of the poor,
unkempt swarms to look upon.
A din of beggars rises up:
the prefect shudders, amazed,
turning upon Lawrence,
threatening with troubled eyes.
Against him the other, gnashing nothing, says,
“Why menacing? Or what displeases you?
Do you reckon these things sordid or cheap,
do you reckon them fit to be spat upon?
The gold for which you ardently thirst,
the dug-up rubble brings forth,
and penal labour hammers it
out of the squalid mines,
or a torrent, a turbid river
rolling, enfolds it in its sands;
what is earthy and sordid
must be boiled down by fire.
Through gold modesty is undone,
by gold integrity is violated,
peace falls dead, faith perishes,
and the laws themselves fall away.
Why do you exalt the poison of glory
and reckon it a great thing?
If you seek truer gold,
it is light, and the human race.
These are the nurslings of light,
whom a feeble body confines,
lest, through the health of the flesh,
the swollen mind grow insolent.
When disease breaks the limbs apart,
the spirit thrives the more robust,
and, when the limbs are strong in turn,
the force of the senses is wounded.
For blood, hot toward sin,
supplies the less strength
if its heat, worn out by wickedness,
draws in a sluggish poison.
If by chance the choice were given,
I would rather, in sharpest pain,
suffer the breaking of my limbs
and live, fair, within.
Set the shapes of disease together
and compare the rival plagues:
is the sickness of the flesh more foul,
or the ulcers of mind and morals?
Our men, through their feeble limbs,
whole in their inward beauty,
bear a harmless sense of grace,
untouched by toil.
Your men, strong in body,
an inward leprosy corrupts,
and error limps, maimed,
and blind fraud sees nothing.
Any one of your princes,
who shine in robe and face,
I will prove more crippled
than any one of my poor men.
This man, who is proud in silk,
whom a chariot carries puffed up,
a watery dropsy stretches
with shining poison within.
But here the miser draws together
his curved hands, and, folding
his palm with hooked nails,
cannot loosen the sinews.
That one, dragged by foul lust
through the public brothels,
mud and sewers defile,
while he begs for filthy debauchery.
What? That one, burning with ambition
and seething with thirst for honour,
does he not gasp in sunken fevers
and rage with the fire of his veins?
Whoever, unrestrained in keeping silence,
itches to betray what should be unspoken,
is tormented and scratches his liver
and bears the itch of his heart.
Why should I lay open the swollen
tumours of envious breasts?
Why the festering and livid
wounds of their malignancies?
You yourself, who rule Rome,
a despiser of the eternal God,
while you worship the filth of demons,
labour under the royal disease.
These, whom you proudly despise,
whom you judge fit for cursing,
will soon put off their ulcerous
limbs and be made whole,
when, freed and loosed at last
from the most corrupted flesh,
in the fairest state of life
they will shine in the Father’s citadel,
not soiled or feeble,
as they seem for now,
but bright in purple robes
and in crowns of gold.
Then, if the chance should offer,
before your very eyes
I would have these mighty men of the age
given over to be reviewed.
You would see them covered in rags
and with snivelling nostrils,
the chin wet with spittle,
and bleared with rotting eyelid.
Nothing is more loathsome than the sinner,
nothing so leprous or putrid;
raw is the scar of his crimes,
and it reeks like the cave of Tartarus.
For souls, by a reversed turn,
a corrupted form is inflicted,
souls that a fair appearance once
had delighted in the body.
Lo, then, the golden coins
which lately I promised,
which no ashes can bury
nor any thief steal away.
Now I add noble gems,
lest you think Christ poor,
gems of glittering light,
with which this temple is adorned.
You see the consecrated virgins,
you marvel at the untouched aged women,
who, after the loss of a first marriage-bed,
know nothing of a second fire.
This is the necklace of the Church,
with these gems she is adorned;
so dowered she pleases Christ,
so she crowns her lofty head.
Behold the talents, take them;
you will adorn the city of Romulus,
you will enrich the prince’s estate,
and you yourself will become richer.”
“We are mocked,” the prefect cries out,
raging, “and in marvellous ways
through so many guises we are played with:
and the madman’s head still lives!
Do you think, you gallows-bird,
that you have woven such great tricks
with unpunished, mimic mockery,
while, a buffoon, you dance your farce?
Did it seem a fine wit
to handle us with jests?
Was I, sold to your laughter,
a festive little turn?
Is there then no severity,
no censure in the fasces?
Has soft gentleness so blunted
the public axe?
You say, ‘I will gladly meet death,
death is the martyr’s wish.’
This is your vanity of persuasion,
we know it well.
But to one who wills it I will not grant
that a swift death’s
short-cut exit be supplied;
I will not let you perish in haste.
I will hold your life and prolong it
with the unbroken penalties of delay,
and an inextricable death
shall draw out long agonies.
Spread out the warm coals,
lest the heat, too fiery,
seize the stubborn man’s face
and enter the hidden places of his heart.
Let the vapour grow faint and languish,
which, poured out with a light breath,
may gradually temper the torments
of the half-burnt body.
It is well that the high priest himself
of them all has fallen here;
he alone will give an example
of what they must soon fear.
Climb the spread-out pyre,
lie down on a worthy little bed;
then, if you please, argue
that my Vulcan is nothing.”
As the prefect speaks this, the savage
torturers on this side and that prepare
to strip the martyr of his garment,
to bind his limbs and stretch them out.
His face shone with beauty,
and a radiance was poured around him.
Such a countenance the lawgiver bore down
when he returned from the mountain,
which the Jewish people, defiled
and discoloured by the golden ox,
feared, and turned their face back,
unable to endure God.
Such glory too did that other
show of a gleaming face,
Stephen, through the shower of stones
gazing on the opened heavens.
This shone from afar
upon the lately cleansed brethren,
whom baptism, newly given,
had made able to receive Christ;
but the blindness of the impious,
their face smeared with the grime of night,
covered beneath a blackening veil,
does not see the brightness,
after the manner of the Egyptian plague,
which, while with darkness it condemned
the barbarians, showed the Hebrews day
in clear light.
Indeed the very quality of the smell
which the scorched skin gives back
moves the two in opposite ways:
to these a stench, to those it is nectar,
and the same sense, varied
by differing air, either afflicts
the nostrils with avenging horror
or soothes with delight.
So God is the eternal fire,
for Christ is the true fire;
he himself fills the just with light
and burns the guilty.
After the long-lasting vapour
had cooked the burnt-out side,
unprompted, from the gridiron he addresses
the judge with a brief speech:
“Turn the part of my body
long since sufficiently roasted,
and make trial of what your
burning Vulcan has done.”
The prefect orders him turned over.
Then he: “It is cooked, devour it,
and take the proof
whether it is sweeter raw or roasted.”
This he had said in sport,
then he looks up to heaven,
and, groaning deeply, he prays,
pitying the city of Romulus:
“O Christ, the only name,
O splendour, O power of the Father,
O maker of earth and sky,
and founder of these walls,
who set the sceptre of Rome
at the summit of things, ordaining
that the world should serve the Quirinal toga
and yield to its arms,
so that the customs of discordant nations,
their observance,
their tongues, their characters, their rites
you might tame under single laws,
lo, beneath the realm of Remus
the whole mortal race has yielded,
discordant rites speak alike,
they feel the selfsame thing.
This was destined, that all the more
the law of the Christian name
might bind whatever land lies open
with a single bond.
Grant, Christ, to your Romans
that the city be Christian,
through which you gave that to the rest
there should be one mind in worship.
All its members are confederated,
from this side and that, into one creed.
The subject world grows gentle;
let the supreme head grow gentle too.
Let it turn the sundered regions
to meet in a single grace;
let Romulus become faithful,
and let Numa himself now believe.
The Trojan error still confounds
the senate-house of the Catos,
venerating at hidden hearths
the exiled household gods of the Phrygians.
Two-faced Janus and Sterculus
the senate worships (I shudder
to name so many monsters of the fathers)
and the feasts of old Saturn.
Wipe away, Christ, this disgrace,
send forth your Gabriel,
that the wandering blindness of Iulus
may acknowledge the true God.
And already we hold most faithful
hostages of this hope,
for here indeed already reign the two
chief among the apostles,
one the caller of the nations,
the other, holding the first chair,
unlocks the entrusted
gates of eternity.
Depart, adulterous Jupiter,
stained with your sister’s defilement,
leave Rome free,
and flee now the people of Christ.
Paul drives you out from here,
the blood of Peter dislodges you;
that which you yourself had armed,
the deed of Nero, works against you.
I see that there will be a prince
some day who, a servant of God,
will not suffer Rome to serve
the foul filth of the rites,
who will bar the temples with bolts,
block up the ivory doors,
condemn the accursed thresholds,
fastening them with bars of bronze.
Then, pure from all blood,
the marbles will gleam at last,
and the bronzes will stand harmless
that now are held as idols.”
This was the end of his praying
and the same the end of the bond
of the flesh: the spirit, willing,
broke forth, following his voice.
Certain fathers bore the body
on their bent necks,
whom the man’s wondrous freedom
had urged to seek out Christ.
A sudden disposition had breathed
into their marrow and compelled them,
through love of the exalted God,
to hate their former trifles.
From that day the worship
of the base gods grew cold:
fewer in the shrines, the people
run to the tribunal of Christ.
So fighting, Lawrence
girt no sword upon his side,
but, turning the enemy’s steel back,
bore it against its author.
While the demon provoked God’s
unconquered witness to battle,
pierced through, he himself fell
and lies laid low forever.
That death of the holy martyr
was the true death of the temples;
then Vesta felt the Palladian household gods
deserted with impunity.
Whatever of the Romans was wont
to pray at Numa’s sacrificial ladle,
thronging the courts of Christ,
echoes the martyr in hymns.
The very luminaries of the senate,
once Luperci or flamens,
kiss the thresholds
of the apostles and martyrs.
We see illustrious houses,
noble in both sexes,
offer in their vows the pledges
of their most renowned children.
The once fillet-crowned pontiff
is enrolled under the sign of the cross,
and a Vestal, Claudia, enters
your temple, Lawrence.
O three and four and seven times
blessed dweller of the city,
who close at hand honours you
and the seat of your bones,
who is permitted to fall down beside them,
who sprinkles the place with weeping,
who presses his breast to the ground,
who pours out his vows in a murmur.
Us the Basque Ebro separates,
set apart by two ranges of Alps,
across the ridges of the Cottian heights,
and across the snowy Pyrenees.
The fame is scarcely known how full
of hidden saints Rome is,
how richly the city’s soil
flowers with sacred tombs.
But we who lack these blessings,
and cannot see the traces
of their blood before us,
gaze on heaven from afar.
So, holy Lawrence, we seek out
your passion:
for you have a twofold hall,
here for your body, in heaven for your mind.
There, chosen as a citizen
of the unutterable city,
in the citadel of the eternal court
you bear the civic crown.
I seem to see the man
glittering with illustrious gems,
whom heavenly Rome has chosen
for herself as everlasting consul.
What power has been entrusted to you
and how great a gift is given,
the joys make proof, for Rome,
which, when asked, you grant.
Whatever each suppliant asks,
he bears it granted, with good success;
they ask, they jest, they tell their need,
and not one returns in sorrow,
as though you were ever present and at hand
and, embracing your city’s nurslings
at your nursing bosom,
fed them with a father’s love.
Among these, O glory of Christ,
hear a rustic poet
confessing the crimes of his heart
and betraying his own deeds.
Unworthy, I acknowledge and know,
that Christ himself should hear me,
but through the patron martyrs
he can obtain a remedy.
Hear kindly the suppliant
Prudentius, a man guilty before Christ,
and, the slave of his body,
absolve him from the chains of the age.
Hymn in Honour of the Passion of Eulalia, Most Blessed Martyr.
Eulalia, noble in her lineage
and nobler in her manner of death,
honours her own Merida, the holy maiden—
the city from whose breast she sprang—
with her bones, and cherishes it in love.
There is a place near the setting sun
that bore this rare distinction,
mighty in its city, rich in peoples,
but mightier in the blood of martyrdom
and powerful by the title of her virginity.
Through three courses and nine
she had four times reached three winters,
when with a crackling pyre she terrified
the trembling, harsh executioners,
counting the torment sweet to her.
She had given proof before
that she stretched toward the Father’s throne
and that her limbs were not dedicated to the marriage-bed:
she had pushed away her very rattles,
a little girl who knew not how to play;
to scorn amber, to spurn roses,
to reject golden necklaces,
stern of face, modest in her step,
and, with manners too tender,
she rehearsed the grey hairs of the old.
But when the maddened plague
rouses itself against the Lord’s servants
and bloodily bids the worshippers of Christ
burn incense, to make smoke
of a beast’s liver to deadly gods,
the holy spirit of Eulalia
roared up, and fierce in temper
prepared to break the turbulent wars,
and, a woman, with breath untrained,
she provokes God to the arms of men.
But the pious care of her mother contrives
that the spirited maiden should hide at home,
concealed in the country and far from the city,
lest the wild girl, in love with death,
should rush to the price of her blood.
She, loathing to bear the relief of rest
with a degenerate delay,
by night, with no witness, stirs the doors
and, escaping, opens the enclosed bars;
then by trackless ways she takes her road.
She sets out with torn feet
through places rough with neglect and brambles,
attended by an angelic choir,
and though the bristling night is silent,
yet she has light for her guide.
So the noble throng of the fathers
had a pillar-bearing ray,
which, able to cut a path through the dark
night with a clear torch,
gave it as chaos passed away.
No otherwise the pious maiden, following
her road by night, deserved the day,
nor was she covered by the darkness,
while she fled the realms of Canopus
and made her way above the stars.
She, swift with sleepless step,
covers many miles before
the eastern region opens the sky;
at morning, proud, she comes to the tribunal,
stands amid the fasces
crying out: “I ask, what madness is it
to destroy souls headlong,
and, hearts wickedly lavish of themselves,
to throw them down on polished crags,
and to deny God the Father of all?
Do you seek, O pitiable band,
the race of Christ’s worshippers? Lo, here am I,
an enemy to the demonic rites;
I trample the idols beneath my feet,
and with heart and mouth I confess God.
Isis, Apollo, Venus are nothing,
and Maximian himself is nothing:
they nothing, because made by hand,
he, because he worships the works of hands,
both frivolous and both nothing.
Maximian, lord of wealth
and yet himself a client of stones,
let him prostitute and vow
his own head to his deities:
why does he shake noble breasts?
A good leader, a rare judge,
he feeds on innocent blood,
and, gaping after pious bodies,
he tears apart sober flesh,
and rejoices to torture faith.
Come then, torturer, burn, cut,
divide my limbs compacted of clay.
To loosen a fragile thing is easy:
the inner mind will not be pierced,
though pain harass it.”
Roused to fury by such words
the praetor says: “Seize the headstrong girl,
lictor, and overwhelm her with torments,
let her feel there are gods of her fathers
and that the prince’s rule is no light thing.
Yet how I would wish, before your death,
if it be possible, to call back
your wickedness, you grim little girl;
look back on what great joys you reap,
which a wedded honour brings you.
Your house, shaken with tears,
follows you, and the anxious
nobility of your line laments
that you die in the tender flower,
so near to dowries and the marriage-bed.
Does the golden pomp of the marriage-couch not move you,
nor the venerable affection of the old,
whom your reckless frailty wounds?
See, the services are ready
of a torturing death:
either you will be struck on the head with a sword,
or your limbs will be torn by beasts,
or, given to smoking torches
and to be wailed over piteously by your kin,
dissolved into ashes you will flow away.
What labour, I ask, is it to flee these?
If a little salt with your fingertips
and a little incense with your fingers
you would, kind maiden, deign to touch,
a grievous punishment will be far away.”
To this the martyr says nothing; but indeed
she roars, and into the tyrant’s eyes
she throws her spittle, then scatters
the images, and the meal set
on the censers she crushes with her foot.
Without delay, two executioners
tear her reed-slender breast,
and the claw strikes her maiden side
on both sides and cuts to the bone,
while Eulalia counts the marks.
“See, you write upon me, Lord;
how it delights to read these letters
that mark your trophies, Christ!
The very purple of the blood drawn forth
speaks the sacred name.”
These things, without weeping or groan,
glad and undaunted she sang;
dread pain is absent from her spirit,
and her limbs, painted with fresh gore,
a warm-flowing fount washes her skin.
Then came the final torture—
not a wounding laceration,
nor the skin ploughed to the rib-cage,
but a flame on every side, with torches,
rages against her flank and breast.
As her fragrant hair had flowed
over her throat, floating on her shoulders,
with which her bashful modesty
and a maiden’s honour might lie hidden,
the covering of her head set in its way,
the crackling flame flies into her face
and, fed through her hair, seizes
her head and rises above its crown;
the maiden, longing for a swift death,
reaches out and drinks the pyre with her mouth.
Then suddenly a dove darts forth,
whiter than snow, seen to leave
the martyr’s mouth and to follow the stars;
this was Eulalia’s spirit,
milk-white, swift, and harmless.
Her neck sinks as the soul departs
and the fiery pyre dies down;
peace is given to the lifeless limbs,
her breath rejoices and exults in the air
and, winged, seeks the lofty temples.
The attendant himself saw the bird
pass openly from the woman’s mouth,
and, stupefied and thunderstruck,
he leaps up and flees his own deeds,
and the lictor himself flees in terror.
Behold, the icy winter heaps up snow
and covers the whole forum,
and at the same time covers the limbs of Eulalia
lying under the frozen sky
like the linen of a little shroud.
Let the love of weeping men give way,
who are wont to celebrate the last rites,
let the tearful service give way:
the very elements, at God’s command,
bear your funeral, O maiden.
Now there is a place at Merida for her tomb,
a famous colony of Vettonia,
which the memorable river Ana
passes by, and, swift with its greening
current, washes the fair walls.
Here, where with clear marble
a kindly brightness lights the halls,
both the stranger and the native,
the venerable earth keeps the relics
and sacred ashes in its bosom.
Above, the gleaming roofs glow red
with little golden panels,
and cut stones variegate the floor,
so that you would think rosy meadows
were reddening with flowers of every kind.
Gather the purple violets
and reap the blood-red crocuses,
the genial winter does not lack these,
and the warming frost loosens the fields,
that it may heap the baskets with flowers.
Give these gifts from leafy boughs,
maiden and boy, give them.
But I, in the midst of the choir,
will bring garlands woven in dactylic measure,
cheap, withered, yet festal.
So it pleases to venerate her bones
and the altar set upon her bones:
she, placed beneath the feet of God,
looks upon these things, and, won by song,
cherishes her own peoples.
Hymn in Honour of the Eighteen Holy Martyrs of Zaragoza.
Twice nine our people keeps, beneath a single
tomb, the ashes of the martyrs:
Zaragoza we call the city
to which so great a thing belongs.
The house, full of mighty angels,
does not fear the ruin of the fragile world,
bearing in its bosom so many gifts at once
to be offered to Christ,
when God, brandishing his glittering right hand,
borne upon a reddening cloud, shall come
to set for the nations a just
balance with even weight.
Roused from the great world, the city,
each one carrying its precious
gifts in baskets, will hasten
to go to meet Christ.
African Carthage will bring forth your bones,
O learned Cyprian, eloquent of speech;
Cordova will give Acisclus and Zoellus,
and three crowns.
You with three gems will offer a fair diadem
to Christ, mother of the pious,
Tarragona, for whom Fructuosus wove
a stitched-together bond,
(this is the name of the gem bound in the band);
beside it gleam twin stones,
and an equal splendour of the two burns
with a glittering fire.
Wealthy Gerona will display the small glory
of Felix in his holy limbs;
our Calahorra will carry both
whom we venerate.
Barcelona, relying on illustrious Cucufas,
will rise, and Narbonne, made beautiful by Paul,
and powerful Arles will hold you,
holy Genesius.
The chief of the towns of the Lusitanians,
the city, seizing the ashes of the adored maiden,
to meet Christ will hold her out
herself to the altar.
The blood of Justus, to whom Pastor clings,
a twofold offering and a double gift,
Complutum will be glad to bring in its lap,
the limbs of two,
Tangier will heap up its Cassian,
the festal monuments of the Massylian kings,
whose ashes drove the conquered nations
to the yoke of Christ.
To each, a few; with three or two,
and perhaps with five, some will be pleasing
as witnesses of Christ, having first
discharged the pledge of their sacrifice:
you will bring back eighteen holy ones,
Zaragoza, zealous for Christ,
your head bound with golden olive,
with the honour of peace.
You alone have prepared for the Lord, to meet him,
more numerous throngs of martyrs,
you alone, most rich in great piety,
enjoy the light.
Scarcely the populous parent of the Punic world,
scarcely Rome herself, set upon her throne,
is worthy, our glory, to surpass you
in this gift.
At all the gates the sacred blood, offered up,
has shut out the race of envious
demons, and driven away the black darkness,
the city purified.
No horror of the shades lurks within,
for the plague, driven off, flees the people;
Christ dwells in all the streets,
Christ is everywhere.
You would believe this a homeland owed
to the martyrs’ sacred crowns, whence a choir, rising,
stretches toward heaven, snow-white with the toga’d
nobility,
thence, O conqueror, your palm was born,
the clergy here brought forth so great a triumph,
here the fillet-crowned house of the priestly
Valerii.
As often as a savage whirlwind, in the storms
of old, made the troubled world tremble,
a sadder fury brought its angers
against this temple,
and no madness departed without praise of ours,
or empty of illustrious blood;
the number of martyrs always grew
beneath every hailstorm.
Did you not, O conqueror, a martyr destined to be slain
abroad, mark for these lands with a thin
dew of blood the likeness of what was to come,
in your nearby death?
This the citizens honour, as though their own
turf enclosed his very limbs and, embracing,
kept in a father’s tomb the bones
of the blessed martyr.
He is ours, although, having suffered far from here
in an unknown city, he gave the glory
of his tomb, a conqueror, near the shore of high
Saguntum, as it chanced.
Ours too, a boy in our wrestling-school,
anointed with the oil of valour and of faith,
learned by his art to tame with strength
the dreadful foe,
he knew the palms won famous in this temple,
eight times and ten times gained;
taught by his country’s laurels, he ran
with the same praise,
here too, Encratis, rest the bones
of your virtues, with which, savage virgin,
you disgraced the spirit
of the violent world.
To none of the martyrs, while life remained,
has it fallen to dwell in our lands;
you alone, surviving your own death,
live in the world.
You live, and unfold the sequence of your suffering,
and, keeping the spoil of your mangled flesh,
you tell what bitter furrows the foul
wounds possess.
The barbarous torturer tore every side,
blood was spent, the limbs were lacerated,
the breast lay open, the nipple cut away
beneath the very heart.
Now of less worth is a death completed,
which, abolishing the venomed pains,
gives to the limbs a hastened rest
with a drowsy end.
A raw scar held you long,
and pain clung burning in your veins for long,
while a wasting humour thinned
your rotting marrow.
Though the persecutor’s envious sword
denied you the final death,
yet, martyr, a full penalty crowns you
as though slain,
we have seen a part of your liver torn away
and lying far off, gripped by the claws:
pale death has something of yours,
though you yet live.
This new title for our Zaragoza to enjoy
Christ himself has given,
that the house might be the consecrated dwelling
of a living martyr,
so, with three times six sacred white-robed ones,
O rich one, with Optatus and at the same time Lupercus,
go on to set forth in psalms the senate
enrolled for you,
name Successus, sing Martialis,
let the death of Urbanus be sung together for you,
let your song echo Julia and at the same time
Quintilianus.
Let the choir name Publius, and recount
what the trophy of Fronto was,
what good Felix bore, what fierce
Caecilianus,
how great a blood, Evotus, stained your wars,
how great yours, Primitivus,
then let lively praise recall your triumphs,
Apodemius.
After these there remains the name of four
men, which the metre refuses to raise up,
whom ancient antiquity records were called
the Saturnini.
The laws of song the love of golden
names sets at little worth, and the care
of speaking about the saints is not faulty
nor ever rude.
It is a measure full of art to recite to Christ
the noted forms of their names,
which the book of heaven holds, to be unfolded
in its due time,
then will the angel recall eight saints and ten
before the Father and the Son,
holding the governance of one city
by right of the tomb.
Indeed to the ancient number will be drawn
the maiden alive after the proof of her suffering,
and the death, O conqueror, which is for you the fount
of blood and of honour,
with Gaius added (for he is not to be passed in silence)
and you, Crementius, to whom it fell
to bear a bloodless glory from a second
contest of praise,
both stood having confessed the Lord
fiercely against the roaring of the robbers,
both lightly tasted the savour
of the martyrdoms.
This throng, set beneath the eternal altar,
prays pardon for our falls,
the throng whom the mother of the purple-robed
nobles keeps,
grant that with pious weeping we may wash through
the furrows of the marbles by which it is covered,
that I may loosen the bonds of my own
fetters of hope,
lay yourself down whole, noble city,
with me upon the holy tombs; then
soon you will follow, with souls and limbs
rising again, whole.
The Passion of Saint Vincent the Martyr.
Blessed martyr, make prosperous
your day of triumph,
on which, as the wage of your blood,
the crown is given you, Vincent.
This day raised you from the darkness
of the age—the torturer and judge overcome—
up to heaven,
and gave you back to Christ, rejoicing.
Now a partner of the angels,
you shine in a glorious robe,
which, an indomitable witness,
you had washed in streams of gore,
when the idol’s henchman,
girt with black laws,
with sword and chains compelled you
to sacrifice to the gods of the nations.
And first he had poured out soft words,
coaxing you gently,
as the wolf, a snatcher about to seize
the calf, first frisks and fawns.
“The greatest king of the world,” he said,
“who bears the sceptre of Romulus,
has decreed that all should serve
the ancient worship of the gods.
You Nazarenes, draw near,
and spurn your raw rite.
These stones, which the prince worships,
appease with smoke and a victim.”
Here Vincent cries out,
a deacon from the sacred tribe,
a minister of the altar of God,
one of the seven milk-white columns;
“Let those deities preside over you,
you may worship stones, you wood,
you, a dead man, become
the high priest of dead gods.
We shall confess the Father, author of light,
and his Son Christ,
who alone is the true God,
Datianus, this we shall confess.”
Here that man, now more disturbed,
“Do you dare, unhappy one,” he says,
“to violate this law of gods and princes
with harsh words,
a law both sacred and public,
to which the human race yields,
and does the impending peril
of your fervid youth not move you?
For receive this decree:
either an altar with incense and turf
must now be prayed at by you,
or death must be paid with your blood.”
He answered from the other side:
“Come then, whatever of strength,
whatever of power you have,
openly I resist—put it forth!
Hear what our word is:
Christ is God, and the Father:
we are his servants and witnesses;
wrest from me my faith, if you can!
Torments, prison, the claws,
and the plate hissing with flames,
and death itself, the last of penalties,
are sport to Christians.
O your empty vanity
and the brute decree of Caesar!
Worthy of your senses,
you bid us worship deities
hewn out by a craftsman’s hand,
forged anew in hollow bellows,
which lack voice, which lack a step,
unmoving, blind, tongueless.
For these, costly shrines
rise in gleaming marble,
for these, the smitten necks
of bellowing bulls fall.
But there too there are spirits,
there are, but masters of crimes,
fowlers after your salvation,
wandering, powerless, filthy,
who secretly drive you, goaded,
into every wickedness,
to ravage the just with slaughter,
to tear at the people of the pious.
They themselves know and feel
that Christ is mighty and lives,
and that his dreadful kingdom
is now, now at hand for the faithless.
In short they cry out, confessing,
driven from the hiding-places of the flesh
by the power and name of Christ,
both the gods and the same demons.”
The profane judge did not bear
the martyr thundering these things.
He cries out: “Stop up his mouth,
lest the shameless man hurl out more.
Shut the voice of the speaker
and hand him swiftly to the lictors,
those Plutos of the accused,
fed on cut-away flesh.
Now I will make the railer feel
the praetorian power,
lest he have mocked at us with impunity
to himself, while our gods are torn down.
Shall for you alone, stubborn one,
the Tarpeian rites be trampled?
Shall you, moreover, alone crush
Rome, the senate, Caesar?
Bound, with his arms twisted back,
stretch him upward and downward,
until the framework of his bones,
torn apart, cracks limb from limb.
After this, with gaping blows
lay bare the hidden parts of his ribs,
that through the recesses of the wounds
his uncovered liver may quiver.”
God’s soldier laughed at this,
rebuking the bloody hands
because the fixed claw did not enter
his limbs more deeply.
And now all the strength of the strong men
had failed in the disembowelling,
and panting effort had loosened
the weary muscles of their arms.
But he, so much the gladder,
lights up his brow, serene,
free of every cloud,
seeing you, Christ, present.
“What a look is that—for shame!”
Datianus said, raging,
“he rejoices, he beams, he challenges,
tortured, fiercer than the torturer!
That force, exercised
on the deaths of so many guilty,
gains nothing in this contest,
and the art of pains is conquered.
But you, nurslings of the prison,
a pair ever unconquered by me,
hold back your right hands a little,
that the weary vigour may breathe.
When the sores are dried again,
while the scar gathers itself
of the cooled blood,
a hand, re-furrowing, will wreck them.”
Against this the deacon replies:
“If now you see the strength
of your hounds grow faint,
come, you yourself, greater butcher,
show by what means they can
split the deepest recesses,
and thrust in your own hand
and drink the boiling streams.
You err, bloody one, if you think
you take your penalty upon me
when you slay the limbs
liable to death, torn to pieces.
There is another, there is one within,
whom none can violate,
free, quiet, whole,
with no share in the grim pains.
This, which you labour to destroy
with such great forces of fury,
is a vessel, loose and of clay,
to be broken in any way.
Indeed, rather, now strive
to cut and punish that one
who stands firm within, who tramples,
tyrant, on your madness.
This one, this one provoke, this one shatter—
unconquered, insuperable,
subject to no storms,
and subject to God alone.”
This he says, and again is mangled
by the hissing hooks,
to whom the praetor with treacherous mouth
hisses out serpent words:
“If such great stubbornness
hardens the callous of your breast
that you abhor to touch
our sacred cushion with your hand,
at least uncover the hidden pages
and the concealed books,
that the sect, sowing what is wicked,
may be burned with righteous fires.”
Hearing this, the martyr says:
“The fire which you, malignant one,
threatening, hold over the mystic letters,
you yourself will burn in, the more justly.
For the avenging sword of the heavenly
volumes will burn through
the tongue, interpreter of so great a poison,
with its thunderbolt.
You see the ashes that betray
the crimes of the men of Gomorrah,
nor is the dust of Sodom hidden,
an everlasting witness of their destruction.
This is your likeness, serpent,
whom soon the soot of sulphur
and bitumen mixed with pitch
will enmesh in lowest Tartarus.”
At this the persecutor, wounded,
turns pale, reddens, seethes,
rolling his mad eyes,
and, gnashing, casts up foam.
Then, having hesitated long,
he decrees: “Let the last examination
of all be plied with fire,
the gridiron, and the plates.”
At this he hurls himself toward the offices
with hastened step,
and, swift with joy, he forestalls
the very ministers of his penalty.
They came to the wrestling-ground of glory,
where hope and cruelty contend,
they join a doubtful struggle,
here the martyr, there the torturer.
A serrated rule roughens the bed
with its scattered teeth,
which a great heap of coals
makes steam with a living breath.
This pyre the holy man mounts
of his own will, with undaunted face,
as though, already conscious of his crown,
he were climbing a lofty tribunal.
Beneath, with crackling spray,
he glitters, sprinkled with shaken salt,
and, boiling with hissing stabs,
is driven scattered through his limbs.
Then the fat, pressed on, washes
the fiery branding-iron,
whence a force of smoking dew
melts gradually into his limbs.
Amid these he remains unmoved,
as though unknowing of pains,
and lifts his eyes on high,
for the bonds had bound his hands.
Raised up the stronger from there,
he is thrust into a mournful cave,
lest the free use of light
should enliven his lofty spirit.
Within, in the deepest dungeon,
is a place blacker with darkness,
which the narrow stones of a sunken vault
strangle, shut up.
Eternal night lurks there,
without the daytime star;
this dreadful prison is said
to have its own underworld.
Into this pit the savage foe
casts the martyr,
and sets his soles in wood,
with his legs spread apart.
Indeed he adds a new penalty too,
a craftsman skilled in the cross,
known to no tyrant
nor heard of in story before.
He orders that fragments of potsherds,
rough, with unpolished corners,
sharp-pointed, shapeless,
be strewn beneath the lying man’s back.
Anxious pains arm the whole couch
with sharp points,
which, beneath his sleepless side,
may strike with a piercing edge to meet him.
These the crafty man, devising
with cunning skill, had set in place,
but Christ destroys the clever
contrivances of Beelzebub.
For the prison’s blindness
flashes with the splendour of light,
and the twofold biting of the stock
leaps apart, its hollows broken.
Here Vincent recognizes
that it is at hand, what he had hoped,
the reward of so great a labour,
Christ, the giver of light.
Then he sees the fragments
of the potsherds now clothe themselves
in soft flowers,
the prison breathing the fragrance of nectar.
Indeed too the thronging angels
stand and speak close at hand,
one of whom, more august of face,
addresses the man with these words:
“Rise, renowned martyr,
rise, secure for yourself,
rise and be added to the kindly
assemblies as our comrade.
Now you have run enough
the offices of menacing punishment,
and, by the fair exit of death,
all your passion is accomplished.
O most unconquered soldier,
stronger than the strongest,
now the savage and harsh torments themselves
tremble at you, the conqueror.
Christ God, the spectator of these things,
repays them with an endless age,
and crowns with a generous right hand
the partner of his own cross.
Lay aside this perishing little vessel
woven of an iron framework,
which, shattered, is dissolved,
and come free into heaven.”
So he; but his inner light
breaks the closed doors,
and a thin brightness, through the cracks,
betrays the hidden light.
When the keeper of the dark threshold,
whom a night-long watch had held
to guard the deadly house,
stood stupefied and terrified at this,
he hears besides the martyr’s
most sweet song of praise,
to which, like a rival voice,
the hollow chamber gives an echo.
Then, fearing, he looks in,
as far as his sight, set against the doorposts,
can enter through the narrow
joints of the hinges.
He sees the strewn potsherds
put forth spring with many flowers,
and the man himself, his bonds torn off,
walking about and singing.
The ears of the troubled praetor
are filled with this miracle;
conquered, he weeps and, groaning, turns over
his anger, grief, and disgrace.
“Taken out of prison,” he says,
“let him be revived a little
with kind warmth, that, refreshed,
he may furnish new food for punishments.”
You might see a faithful crowd
gathering from the whole town,
softening his propped-up couch,
drying his raw wounds.
One wanders over the twofold furrows
of the claws with his kisses,
this one rejoices to lick the empurpling
gore of his body.
Many a linen garment they fashion
with the dripping blood,
that they may keep it at home
as a sacred safeguard for their descendants.
Then the very master of the prison
and the keeper of the chains,
as conscious antiquity reports,
suddenly believed in Christ.
He had seen, with the bolts barred,
the cave of dense gloom
gleam, shut up, with the splendour
of a stranger light.
But indeed, after the martyr
reached the rest of the couch,
sick with the weariness of delays
and kindled with the thirst of death—
if such a thing is to be called death,
which from the body’s dungeon
releases the free mind
and gives it back to God its author,
a mind cleansed by blood,
washed clean in the lavers of death,
which offered itself and its own life
to be sacrificed to Christ—
so then, as he leaned back his head
on the soft hangings thrown aside,
his spirit, leaving his limbs,
a conqueror, seizes heaven.
For him a way is unbarred,
straight, by a lofty path, to the Father,
which blessed Abel, slain by his impious
brother, had climbed.
White-robed choirs of the saints
throng him as he goes, on this side and that,
and John the Baptist, sent forth
from a like prison, calls him.
But the foe of the Christian name
was being scorched: the vain poisons
of his gall and his livid heart
had burned him out, made savage.
You would believe a dragon raged,
unarmed, its teeth broken.
“He escaped, exulting,” he says,
“the rebel, and bore off the palm.
But that last thing remains,
to inflict punishment on the dead,
to hand the corpse to the beasts
or give it to the dogs to tear.
Even now I will blot out his bones,
lest there be a tomb for his body
which the common herd may honour
and mark a martyr’s title.”
So he gnashes, and the holy body
the profane man (ah, dread crime!),
naked, its covering denied,
exposes among the sedge.
But none of the dread famine,
or of beasts or of birds,
dares to defile the trophy
of glory with a foul touch.
Indeed, if any, screaming shamelessly,
had flown around it from afar,
driven off by the onset
of a fierce bird, it turned to flight.
For a raven, once given to Elijah
as a carrier of food,
fulfils this duty diligently
and keeps watch close by.
From the nearby thickets it,
hostile with the sound of its wings,
and lashing the eyes with its feathers,
drove off the monstrous wolf.
Who of the faithless would dare to believe
that a rapacious beast,
ready to grapple with bulls,
gave way to soft feathers?
It went, growling its malice,
terrified by the bird’s light flight,
and had fled the prey it had seen
at the threats of an unwarlike guard.
What was your feeling then, Datianus,
as you heard such things?
With what great stabs did a hidden grief
pierce you, groaning,
when you saw yourself conquered
by the power of a slain body,
and unequal even to the very bones,
and lesser now than the empty limbs?
But what end, stubborn tyrant,
will set a limit to this
unbridled spirit?
Will no measure break you?
“None, nor will I ever cease;
for if savage ferocity
grows gentle, and clemency
softens the devouring ravens,
I will sink the corpse in the waves:
the mad wave never pardons
the shipwrecked, and the foaming
deep knows not how to spare.
Either it will always be borne there,
shifting through uncertain mockeries,
by wandering blasts,
feeding the scaly throngs,
or beneath the broken crags
the rough spines of the rocks
will burst the torn flesh
among the jagged recesses.
Is there any of the men, skilled
to drive a boat with vigour
by oar, rope, and sail,
who can cut the sea,
who may snatch from the marshy turf
the body that lies untouched,
and, carried in a light skiff,
bear it away over the broad expanse?
But let a hempen sack
enclose the folded corpse,
which a stone, tied by a cord,
may sink headlong into the deep.
And do you dart forth over the waves,
swift with the dripping oar-blade,
until a longer distance
hides the abandoned land from sight.”
A certain one of the soldiers
(Eumorphio was his name),
violent, bold, barbarous,
seizes these orders, hot with fury.
He weaves the corded mat,
fills it with the sewn-up body,
and, having measured much of the strait,
shakes it out amid the storms.
O most mighty power of God,
creating power of all things,
which once had levelled the swelling sea
as Christ walked upon it,
so that, treading the back of the deep,
he passed with dry steps,
and the wayfarer of the vast abyss
wet not his soles in the waves!
This same power had ordered
the Red Sea to gape open,
while, the floor laid bare,
the people, secure, tread a dry road.
So now too it bids
the sea serve the holy body
with quiet glidings,
sloping toward the curving shores.
A stone of millstone weight,
like white foam, floats up,
and the basket, guardian of so great
a pledge, is borne upon the waves.
The sailors, amazed, behold it
carried over the re-measured deep,
gliding gently backward,
with favourable tide and wind.
They themselves too contend to cut
the sea with their swift vessel,
but the limbs far outstrip them
to the soft bosom of the land;
in short, the quiet earth
receives them, brought back first,
before the keel, driven by their utmost
efforts, could touch the harbour.
Happy that retreat of the pleasant
shore, which, cherishing the holy
flesh in its sands,
served in place of a tomb,
while the pious care of the saints,
weeping, adorns the mound
and, the body entrusted to the tomb,
keeps it for the life to come!
But soon, the enemies subdued,
when peace was now restored to the just,
an altar grants the due rest
to the blessed bones;
for, set beneath the sanctuary
and laid up at the very foot of the altar,
they drink, drenched below,
the air of the heavenly gift.
So the body; but the seat of God
itself contains the man, received
with the Maccabee brothers
and next to Isaiah, who was sawn asunder,
yet to them fell a simple
crown of their pains, for whom
the final exit of death
set an end to their evils.
What such thing did the dismemberer dare?
Did he cast the severed segments
of the body, after the saw, to the beasts,
or give them to the waves?
Did the tyrant offer the tongue
of the Maccabee martyr, torn out,
or the skin snatched from his head,
to the bloody birds?
You alone, O twice-renowned,
you alone bore off the palm
of a double prize, you prepared
two laurels at once.
A conqueror in harsh death,
then afterward, after death, a conqueror
with equal triumph, you trample
the robber down with your body alone.
Be present now and receive
the suppliant voices of those who pray,
an effective pleader of our guilt
before the throne of the Father.
By yourself, by that prison,
the increase of your honour,
by the bonds, the flames, the claws,
by the prison’s stock,
by that potsherd fragment,
by which your won glory grew,
and the couch which we, trembling
descendants, kiss,
have pity on our prayers,
that Christ, appeased, may incline
a favourable ear to his own
and not charge all our sins.
If duly we venerate the solemn day
with mouth and heart,
if beneath the joy of your
footsteps we are laid low,
glide hither for a little while,
bringing the favour of Christ,
that our burdened senses may feel
the relief of pardon.
So let no delay now remain,
but that the noble spirit may take up
the flesh, roused again,
endowed with equal power,
so that the flesh which, sharing the labours,
bore the common peril,
may be also co-heir of glory
through all the ages forever.
Hymn in Honour of the Most Blessed Martyrs Fructuosus, Bishop of the Church of Tarragona, and Augurius and Eulogius, Deacons.
Happy Tarragona, Fructuosus, by your fires
lifts up its head, glittering,
shining from afar with two deacons.
God looks kindly upon the Spaniards,
since the powerful Trinity crowns
the Spanish citadel with a threefold martyr.
Burning Augurius seizes the heavens,
and Eulogius too, at the same time, radiant,
stretches toward the throne of Christ on high.
Their leader, going before, and their master
toward so great a glory, illustrious
in his episcopal name, was Fructuosus,
for, summoned suddenly by the governor’s
command, the priest had come to the forum
with his two deacons accompanying him.
Then to the prison’s chain the executioner,
fed on blood, was dragging the men;
Fructuosus rejoices to run forward of his own will.
And, lest any fear should strike his companions,
the vehement teacher strengthens them as they go
and kindles their faith with the warmth of Christ.
“Stand with me, men. The bloody serpent
calls God’s ministers to their punishment;
let not death frighten you; the palm is prepared.
Prison, for Christ’s worshippers, is a step to the crown,
prison carries them up to the heights of heaven,
prison reconciles God to the blessed.”
With these words they enter the cave of the accused,
they perform there the mystic washing,
and the darkness is amazed at the cleansing of the water.
Here for six continuous days they lie hidden;
at last they stand before the savage enemy’s tribunal:
the racks tremble at the three brothers.
The judge Aemilianus loomed over them,
fierce, turbulent, insolent, profane;
he ordered the demonic altars to be worshipped.
“You who, a teacher,” he says, “sow a new
kind of fiction, so that fickle girls
forsake the groves and abandon Jupiter,
condemn, if you are wise, this old wives’ dogma.
It is commanded by the mouth of Caesar Gallienus
that what the prince worships, all of us should worship.”
To him speaking thus the calm priest replies:
“I worship the eternal prince of days,
the maker and lord of Gallienus,
and Christ, sprung from the everlasting Father,
whose servant I am, and the shepherd of his flock.”
Smiling, that man says: “You were such once.”
Nor does his fury delay or curb its anger,
he dooms them to be burned in savage fires.
They exult and forbid the crowd to weep.
The priest sees some of the people
offering him a cup to sip:
“We are fasting,” he says; “I refuse the drink:
not yet does the ninth hour unseal the day;
never will I violate the dedicated law,
nor will death itself dissolve my holy rule.
So Christ, thirsting beneath the hour of the cross,
refusing the cup offered to him
and unwilling to taste, carried his thirst through.”
Meanwhile they enter a place shut in
by a rounded cage, soaked with the blood
of many beasts, which fury frequents,
when bloody spectacles resound
and a worthless gladiator, struck
by the hard sword, falls, and pleasure roars.
Here, with a blazing pyre, a black minister,
ordered to prepare the burning punishment,
built up the pyre with the final torches,
who, while he frees the bodies to be burned,
might release their souls, fervent with the love of light,
from the broken cave of the prison.
The pious companions vie in their services:
with the sandals loosed from his feet,
one, bending down, was eager to draw them off,
but holy Fructuosus forbids his bowed
face to be pressed upon: “Be gone,” he says,
“nor let your service burden my death.
Rather I myself will loosen my own feet,
lest my steps, hindered by the bonds,
rush into the fire with slow paces.
Why do laments wet your dripping cheeks?
Why do you ask that I be mindful of you?
For all the peoples I shall ask Christ.”
Scarcely had he said this when he himself loosens
the coverings of his feet, as Moses
once had done, drawing near to the bush.
It was not permitted to tread on the sacred burning
or to stand before God
before pure feet were set forward.
He stood with bare heel: lo, behold,
his spirit leaps up to heaven and sows a saying
which made all who heard it tremble:
“It is not, believe me, a punishment that you see,
which, hastened, passes in a thin moment,
nor does it snatch away life, but reshapes it.
Happy the souls to whom it falls
to climb on high to the Thunderer through fire,
whom one day the everlasting fire will flee.”
Amid these words they enter with swift steps
the crackling hearths, and threaten
the very trembling furnaces of the flames.
At last the bonds, which had drawn back their hands,
bound behind upon their backs,
fall away, burned, the skin untouched.
The punishment did not dare to hold back the palms,
to be raised to the Father in the manner of the cross;
it loosed the arms that they might pray to God.
You would think it the likeness of the three of old,
whom once, singing through the Babylonian fire,
the trembling tyrant beheld amazed.
But the pious flame then spared them,
the time of their passion not yet ripe,
and Christ not yet beginning the glory of death.
When the steaming heat shrank from these,
they pray that swift fire might fly to them
and give an end to their anxious perils.
Entreated, the Majesty at last bids
his servants to die, sent forth
from their perishing bodies and given back to himself.
An attendant from the governor’s house saw
heaven lie open to the martyrs
and the glorious men borne through the stars.
Indeed, warning his master’s little daughters,
he showed the mark of his father’s crime,
that those whom the forum slew live in heaven.
Then virginity was granted openly to see these things
through the clear sky, while the parent was blind,
that the house might fear its lord’s crime.
Then from the holy bodies the ashes
and the bones, drenched with wine, are gathered,
which in haste each one claimed for himself.
So great was the brethren’s love to carry home
the dedicated gifts of the holy ashes,
or to bear the faithful pledge in their bosom.
But lest they should divide among separate tombs,
in different places, the relics that must be raised again
and that soon will be with the Lord together,
they are seen, clad in snow-white robes,
commanding that the dust to be consecrated be restored
and shut up, mingled, in a hollow of marble.
O threefold honour, O three-formed summit,
by which the head of our city is exalted,
eminent above all the Spanish cities!
It is fitting to exult in three patrons,
by whose protection we are all cherished,
the peoples of the Pyrenean lands.
Let a choir of both sexes stand around;
hero, maiden, boy, old man, old woman,
sing duly the psalm of your Fructuosus.
Let the hymn echo, praising Augurius,
matching Eulogius with mingled measures;
let us render equal songs to equals.
Here let the gilded roofs sound in the citadel,
there let the soothing murmur of the shore arise,
and let the holiday seas compose a song.
One day there will be a time, as the world falls,
when Fructuosus, covering you, Tarragona,
from the fire, will free you from sharp torment.
Perhaps he will deign to give a remedy too
to my torments, with Christ’s favouring grace,
as he turns over these sweet hendecasyllables.
Hymn in Honour of Quirinus the Martyr, Bishop of the Church of Siscia.
A man eminent in merit,
Quirinus, pleasing to God,
the walls of the city of Siscia
cherish in a father’s embrace,
a martyr granted to themselves.
Here, under the commander Galerius,
who then pressed the Illyrian regions
with his dominions,
he is said to have made the catholic faith
illustrious through his death.
No hardness of the sword,
no fires, no wild beasts
slay him with a cruel destruction,
but a whirlpool, with its river-waters,
while it sweeps him off, washes him clean.
It matters nothing whether the passion
dyes the martyr in a glassy expanse
or in a river of blood;
his glory comes forth alike,
wet with whatever wave.
From the top of a steep bridge
the bishop of the holy people
is cast headlong into the river,
bearing, hung from a noose,
the stone of a great mill.
The most gentle eddy of the stream
receives him cast down
and does not suffer him to be sunk,
sustaining the vast weight of the stone
with wondrous swimmings.
From afar, from the ground, the frightened
flocks watch their teacher;
for the thronging people of Christ
had hedged the windings of the banks
with a crowded column.
But Quirinus, when, rising up,
he turned his face about, alas, sees his own
people trembling at his example,
himself nothing mindful of his own
peril amid the waters.
He strengthens the pious hearts,
asking with gentle words
that such things should frighten no one,
nor should steadfast faith waver,
nor reckon it a punishment to die.
As he speaks, the river bears his back
over its restless shallows,
nor does the depth spread beneath
dare of its own accord to gape open
for the stone, the noose, and the man.
The martyr bishop felt
that the now-won palm of death
and of his passing was being snatched from him,
and that his ascent was denied
to the throne of the eternal Father.
“Jesus almighty,” he says,
“by no means is this glory
unwonted or new to you,
to trample the roaring of the sea
and to halt the headlong rivers.
We know that the disciple Peter,
when he dipped his steps,
trembling, with a mortal foot,
by the help of your right hand
set the deep beneath solid ground.
The Jordan too we know,
wandering with twisted eddies,
while it is borne in rapid rush,
fled back to its source
by reversed channels.
These are the miracles of your
power, Lord, so that even now
I am held up, lightly floating
on the river’s topmost current,
though I drag a crag at my neck.
Now the proof of you is full
and the power of your name betrayed,
which heathen stupor dulls:
release, I pray, most kind one,
now the delays of this soul.
What you can do the river’s water proves,
which bears up the flint;
this that yet remains I yield,
than which nothing is more precious,
to die for you, Christ God.”
As he prays, at once breath
and voice and warmth desert him;
his spirit climbs the heights,
the stone becomes a heavy weight,
and the waters receive his body.
On the Place where the Martyrs Suffered, now the Baptistery at Calahorra.
A place chosen for Christ it is, where it may carry tried hearts
up to heaven by blood, and cleanse them by water.
Here two men, slain for the Lord’s name,
bore their purple martyrdom by a fair death.
Here too indulgence flows in a clear fount
and washes away old stains in a new stream.
Whoever longs to climb to heaven’s eternal kingdom,
let him come hither thirsting; behold, the way is prepared.
Before, the crowned witnesses climbed the steep
halls; now the washed souls seek the heights.
The Spirit, wont to descend in an everlasting glide,
as it had given the palm, so grants pardon,
the earth drinks the sacred dews, whether from the fount or from blood,
and, wet, overflows forever for its own God.
The lord of the place is he from the wound of whose two sides
on this side blood poured out and flowed, and on that, water,
from here you will go, as each one can, through the wounds of Christ,
borne up, one by swords and another by waters.
The Passion of Saint Cassian of Forum Cornelii.
Cornelius Sulla founded a Forum; this the Italians call a city
from the very name of its founder,
here, as I journeyed toward you, Rome, greatest of all things,
a hope arose in me that Christ would be favourable.
Stretched on the ground, I rolled before a tomb which the holy
martyr Cassian adorns with his consecrated body.
While, weeping, I reckon with myself my wounds and all
the labours of my life and the sharp points of my griefs,
I raised my face to heaven, and there before me stood
an image of the martyr, painted with bright colours,
bearing a thousand blows, lacerated through all his limbs,
showing his skin torn with tiny punctures,
countless boys around him—a pitiable sight—
pierced his pricked limbs with little styluses,
with which they had been wont to run over the wax of their tablets,
writing the murmur of the schoolroom that they were noting down.
The sacristan, when consulted, says: “What you see, stranger,
is no empty or old wives’ tale;
the picture relates a history which, handed down in books,
shows the true faith of an ancient time.
He had presided over the studies of boys and, hedged about
by a great flock, had sat as a master of letters,
skilled to grasp all words in brief notes,
and swiftly to follow what was said with flying marks,
his precepts, sometimes harsh and seeming grim,
had moved the youthful crowd with anger and with fear.
For a teacher is always bitter to the learning youth,
nor is the discipline of childhood sweet to any.
Behold, a savage tempest, shaking the faith, pressed
upon the people dedicated to the Christian glory.
He, the guide of his pupil-flock, is dragged out
from the midst of the assembly, because he had scorned to pray at the altars.
When the deviser of punishments asked what kind of craft
the man knew, so rebellious in his lofty spirit,
they answer: “He governs a tender, boyish band,
training them to mark words with invented signs.”
“Lead him,” he cries out, “lead the captive, and of his own
let the scourger be given over to the little ones themselves,
that they may mock him as they please, may tear him with impunity,
and dye their hands, given holiday, in the master’s blood.
It is a pleasure that the master himself, who has
too harshly constrained them, should furnish the pupils their sport.”
His hands are bound behind his back, his garment stripped away,
and a band comes, armed with sharp styluses.
However much hatred each had conceived in silent anger,
he pours it out, burning, with gall at last set free,
some hurl the fragile tablets and break them
in his face, the wood splits, struck back against his brow,
the waxed boxwood cracks, dashed against his bloody cheeks,
and the page, shortened and wet, reddens from the blow.
Then others brandish goads and iron points,
on the part where the wax is written with ploughed furrows,
and where the cut letters are erased and the rough surface
of the field, gleaming again, is renewed.
On this side Christ’s confessor is dug, on that he is cut;
one part enters the soft flesh, one part splits the skin,
two hundred hands alike pierced all his limbs,
and as many drops of wounds drip at once,
the greater torturer was the child who had pricked the surface,
than he who had bored through the deep flesh;
for the one, a light striker, since death is denied,
knows how to rage with the stabs of pain alone,
while the other, the more deeply he strikes the hidden seats of life,
gives the more relief, since he brings death near.
“Be strong, I pray, and conquer your years by your strength;
what age may grant, let cruelty supply.”
But the tender, weak one labours, his efforts ill-made;
the torments grow while the executioner tires.
“Why do you groan?” one cries out; “you yourself, master,
gave this iron and armed our hands.
See, we give you back as many thousands of marks
as we, standing and weeping at your teaching, received.
You cannot be angry that we write; you yourself bade
that the right hand should never bear a resting stylus,
we do not ask, greedy teacher, for the school-holidays
so often denied us while you were our master,
it pleases us to set down the dots and weave furrows in furrows,
to entangle the bent strokes with chains.
You may correct the verses, inspected in long order,
if perchance a faulty hand has erred in anything.
Exercise your authority: you have the right to punish the fault,
if any of your own has marked you too slackly.”
Such things the boys made sport of upon the master’s limbs,
nor did the long punishment release the weary man,
at last Christ, pitying him as he struggled, from heaven
bids the bonds of his breast be loosed,
and relaxes the hard delays of his soul and the tethers
of his life, and frees its narrow hiding-places,
the blood, following the open ways from the inner
fount of his veins, forsakes his heart,
and through so many openings of his pierced body departs
that vital warmth of his fibres, gasping out.
These are the things which, set forth in clear colours, stranger,
you marvel at; this is the glory of Cassian,
lay before him, if you have any just or lovely vow,
if you have any hope, if you seethe with anything within.
Believe me, the most prosperous martyr hears all prayers,
and grants fulfilled those which he sees worthy.”
I obey, I embrace the tomb, I pour out tears too,
the altar grows warm with my mouth, the stone with my breast.
Then I review all the secret things of my toil,
then I murmur what I was seeking, what I was fearing,
and the home left behind me under a doubtful lot,
and my hope of future good, perhaps wavering.
I am heard, I reach the city, I enjoy favourable success:
I return home, I proclaim Cassian.
The Sayings of Saint Romanus the Martyr against the Heathen.
Romanus, brave champion of Christ the God,
move the organ of my tongueless mouth, my patron,
grant a polished song to one most unskilled in speech,
make me sing in harmony the wonders of your praises,
for you yourself know that the dumb can be made to speak.
A savage torturer tore out the quill of your palate
and throat, yet did not enjoin silence
upon the mouth with which you confessed God.
The voice that witnesses to truth cannot be quenched,
not even if it throbs with its passages cut away.
So our halting speech, with a feeble tongue,
stammers and labours in discordant measures,
but if you sprinkle the heart with heavenly dew
and water the breast with spiritual milk,
a hoarse voice will loosen its hindered sounds.
The evangelist wrote that the Messiah himself
gave such precepts to the apostles:
“Do not, when my mystery is to be
proclaimed, seek out your words with forethought;
I will supply to the unprepared what they shall speak.”
I myself am dumb, but mighty in eloquence
my tongue, Christ, will speak clearly.
He himself will explain what tumults the demon,
with his last breath, while he is being tamed, has stirred up,
a worse plague in his fury at the very end.
So a serpent, wounded by the stroke of a dart,
bites back at the iron, and, fiercer with pain,
lingers, shaking it, with clenched teeth,
but the shaft stays fixed the deeper,
and it feels no vain peril of its bites.
Galerius, as it chanced, ruled the state of the Roman
world as commander, as antiquity reports,
cruel, savage, harsh, implacable.
He had sent edicts far and wide into all the world,
that whoever would rather live should deny Christ.
This the serpent dictates with a royal mouth,
who, coming forth from the tombs of the dead,
cries out: “Why before the time, by your swift coming,
do you dissolve my realms? Spare me, Son of the Highest,
or bid me at least possess the hearts of swine.”
The prefect, intent on these affairs,
Asclepiades, commands his soldiers to go
and to drag the churchman straight from the sanctuaries,
a people to be handed over to chains
unless it should spurn the Nazarene discipline.
Soon, thinking to burst into the temple himself
and eager to ravage the holy of holies,
the profane man, with impious arms, made ready
to lay the altar’s shrine utterly low
and to break the very doors into ruin.
A herald runs ahead, these things being suddenly known,
Romanus, a hero of keen excellence,
announces that the enemies are coming in arms,
forearming the spirits of the fearful with exhortations,
that they may stand ready and not yield to the whirlwind.
The Christian flock conspires, leagued
in one spirit, an undaunted band
of mothers, men, little ones, and virgins;
fixed and settled in all is the resolve
to guard the faith or gladly to die.
The soldier, repulsed, reports back to the benches
that Romanus is the leader of the rebellious people,
that all blaze with stubborn boldness,
that they obstinately offer their bared throats,
so that the strong may meet a glorious death.
Romanus is thereupon ordered to be seized in haste
and, as the sole instigator and torch of all,
to plead the cause on behalf of the defiant people,
he goes without resisting and asks to be bound,
and of his own accord twists his bent hands behind his back.
Love of the crown almost forestalls the savage
art of the lictor, offering of its own will his bared
ribs to be cut by the cloven claws.
He bursts in over the high threshold and, while the heralds
are dumb with amazement, he himself drags the torturer along.
To him standing before him the tyrant thus begins:
“Infamous monster, vile, accursed,
you, agitator of the city and flighty storm
of the crowd, you stir up their unstable minds,
that the ignorant mob may not yield to the laws.
Something popular, under the colour of glory,
the unlettered throng has believed,
that they will be consecrated through the ages
